title: Availability Bias
hook: A fresh storm photo can redraw a whole risk map before the numbers arrive.
coreIdea: Availability bias makes vivid, recent, or emotional examples feel more common or important because memory retrieves them first.
counterintuition: The example you remember fastest is not necessarily the evidence that represents the situation best. A strong decision asks what the data would look like if memory were quieter.
tryThisNow: Write the example that comes to mind first. Then find one base rate or log that represents the whole set.
keyTakeaway: Treat easy recall as a warning light, then check representative evidence before deciding.

breakdown.fastRead:
A storm track is still open on the diamond broker's screen when Rebecca reviews the first offer. Last week's flood story is everywhere, so one threatened mine feels like the whole market. The offer has not changed. Her memory has.

Availability bias appears when the mind mistakes easy recall for real weight. A vivid example comes forward quickly, so it feels frequent, likely, or decisive. Quiet evidence waits in the file.

Memory is a loud clerk, not a fair sample.

The correction is to name the vivid example, then force a count, base rate, log, or comparison that covers the whole set.
breakdown.deepRead:
The storm track on Rebecca's screen shows a red curve near a mining region. The buyer on the phone says prices will jump by Monday. Rebecca can picture the flooded road from a news clip. That image makes the first offer feel urgent, even though the supply report covers twenty mines and only one is near the storm.

Availability bias is not stupidity. It is a useful memory system doing a job too quickly. The mind brings up what is vivid, recent, emotional, or repeated. That helps when a smell warns you about smoke or a near miss changes how you cross a street. The problem starts when the easy example pretends to represent the whole pattern.

A clear image can bully a dull table.

The practical move is to ask what kind of evidence would be less vivid but more representative. For Rebecca, that means production volume, alternate supply, shipment delays, and past storm price moves. For a safety team, it may mean incident logs instead of the crash everyone saw on video. For a manager, it may mean payroll records instead of the employee story that made the room angry.

A language school shows the same mechanism with no storm at all. Patrick is holding a maintenance key after a student named Karina fails the advanced placement interview. The name makes him think of the letter K test: words beginning with K come to mind more easily than words where K sits third, even when the hidden count is larger. Patrick writes letter K on the key tag and checks the last fifty placements before lowering the level cutoff.

Recall speed is not frequency.
breakdown.fullRead:
The food bank loading bay smells of onions, diesel, and wet cardboard. Manon has a booking ledger for three trucks, and everyone is talking about the pantry that ran out of infant formula on Tuesday. The story is vivid because the volunteer cried on the phone. Manon writes risk map across the ledger before sending every truck to that pantry.

This bias builds a risk map from whatever memory can fetch quickly. Airplane crashes, tornadoes, shark attacks, and dramatic fires occupy more mental space than many quieter dangers because images and stories travel well. Meanwhile, routine shortages, chronic illnesses, falls, and small repeated failures can look smaller than they are because they do not arrive as a scene.

Tversky and Kahneman's work on availability made the pattern famous with the letter K: people could more easily think of words that start with K than words with K in the third position, so ease of recall pulled judgment away from the real count. That small puzzle shows a large habit. What comes to mind first feels like what happens most.

What would the answer be if nothing vivid had happened this week?

Manon uses that question on the food bank ledger. The infant-formula story stays on the table. It matters. But she adds delivery counts, waitlists, missed routes, and age-group demand for every pantry. The truck plan changes. One truck goes to the Tuesday pantry, one to a site with a larger silent shortage, and one to a route that had missed two deliveries without a dramatic call.

You can feel the same pressure in a tenant meeting. You are holding a grant rubric when Diego tells the room about a ceiling collapse in one building. The story is awful and immediate. It also threatens to consume the entire repair budget. Diego marks vivid example on the rubric and asks for complaint severity, unit count, and inspection dates across all buildings before ranking repairs.

This pause can feel cold, especially when the case involves harm. It is not cold. It is how you prevent one visible injury from hiding ten less visible ones.

The trap is especially dangerous in operational risk because the memorable event often comes with faces, names, and blame. A crash with video feels bigger than a hundred near misses in a spreadsheet. A missed payroll bonus feels bigger when the angriest employee is in the room. A food shortage feels bigger when the caller cries. Those scenes deserve attention, but they do not deserve sole authority.

So give the vivid case a place, not the whole map. Write it down. Then ask for the boring evidence: counts, logs, base rates, denominators, and missed cases. If the vivid example is truly representative, the broader evidence will confirm it. If it is not, the broader evidence will keep your decision from chasing the easiest memory.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Availability bias turns memorable cases into false maps. Readers need to notice the vivid example and then demand evidence that represents the full set.

examples.title: Patrick Counts Placements Before Cutting

examples.scenario: "Karina froze in the advanced interview," the teacher says as Patrick clips a maintenance key back onto the language-school board. The failed interview is fresh, and the staff wants to lower the cutoff. Patrick has to choose whether one easy-to-recall student should guide the rule, so he writes letter K on the key tag.
examples.whatToDo: Review the last fifty placements, pass rates, and later transfers before changing the cutoff. Use the remembered student as a prompt, not as the count.
examples.whyItMatters: The letter K reminder keeps ease of recall separate from frequency. One vivid placement failure should not rewrite the level system.

examples.scenario: You are in the municipal chamber at 6:20 p.m. holding the grant rubric when Diego, the housing officer, describes a ceiling collapse in Building C. The room goes silent. The story is vivid enough to swallow the repair list. Before the vote, Diego must decide whether to fund the loudest case first or score all buildings by severity, unit count, and inspection date.
examples.whatToDo: Place the collapse inside the rubric and rank it with the full complaint and inspection record. Do not let vividness replace triage.
examples.whyItMatters: A vivid example deserves urgency, but it still needs comparison. The rubric keeps memory from becoming the whole budget.

examples.title: Alice Finds the Quiet Hotspot

examples.scenario: It took Alice two crash photos at the 7:15 a.m. bike-share depot review to notice the fuel receipt was the only dull object in the packet. The Harbour Street photos were everywhere online. The receipt came from a van that serviced a less visible hill route. As operations analyst, Alice marks operational risk on the receipt and must decide whether photos or incident density choose the next fix.
examples.whatToDo: Map crashes per ride and service history by route before assigning crews. Use the viral photos as a signal to inspect, not as the risk map.
examples.whyItMatters: Public images can make one hotspot feel dominant. Operational risk lives in rates, exposure, and repeated near misses.

planSpec.stakes: pay fairness and morale get misallocated if availability bias is treated as a slogan

examples.scenario: Which bonus rule failed, the prototype or the story everyone remembered? Karim answers after payroll closes by putting the prototype form beside the complaint log. One angry supervisor's example had dominated the test. Karim marks bias on the prototype and rebuilds the next bonus review from all missed payouts.
examples.whatToDo: Count every missed payout by role, shift, and rule condition before changing the bonus design. Keep the loud complaint in the set, not above it.
examples.whyItMatters: The remembered complaint may expose a real flaw. It still cannot represent the whole payroll system until the count supports it.

questions.prompt: When availability-bias pressure appears, a hospital team fears a rare drug reaction after a recent case. The medication also prevents many common complications. Which move best avoids availability bias?
choices: Also prevents many supports a narrower read of hospital team fears; keep rare drug reaction central and leave after recent medication aside.
Compare reaction rates, prevented complications, and patient risk groups before changing protocol.
Complications move best fits the immediate pressure around drug reaction after; hold team fears rare steady and test pressure appears hospital later.
questions.explanation: The recent case deserves attention, but protocol should follow rates and tradeoffs. Ignoring the case or letting it dominate both fail.
questions.whyItMatters: Availability Bias turns appears hospital into a shortcut, so the room can overweights team fears while missing rare drug. Compare reaction rates, prevented complications, and patient risk groups before changing protocol protects the decision from that drift.

reviewCards.front: A vivid story comes to mind first. What should you ask before acting?
reviewCards.back: Ask what count, base rate, log, or comparison would represent the full set.

reviewCards.front: Why does availability bias distort risk?
reviewCards.back: Memory retrieves vivid, recent, or emotional cases quickly, so they feel more common than they may be.

reviewCards.front: A dramatic complaint dominates a meeting. What is the corrective move?
reviewCards.back: Put the complaint into the full record and check whether it represents the pattern.

reviewCards.front: What does the letter K example teach?
reviewCards.back: Ease of recall can mislead frequency judgment. What comes to mind faster is not always more common.

reviewCards.front: When is a memorable example useful?
reviewCards.back: It is useful as a prompt to investigate. It becomes dangerous when it replaces representative evidence.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to treat memorable examples as prompts and then check representative evidence before changing a risk map, budget, or rule.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a recent incident dominates my judgment, then I will ask for the rate or log that shows whether it represents the whole risk.
If one story makes the room emotional, then I will write it down and request the count of similar and opposite cases before voting.
If a review or story is easy to remember, then I will compare it with aggregate failure rates before changing my choice.
If a visible failure pulls resources toward one site, then I will check exposure, backlog, and incident counts across all sites first.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, catch one decision driven by a memorable example. Write the example, then find one count or base rate before acting.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, review a risk you may be overestimating or underestimating and rebuild it from logs instead of memory.
